Okay, tell me then why there's no native Windows compatibility layer? IMO it's the only obstacle in its way to become the default home desktop system. Face the facts - most PC users are casuals, and most casual applications are written for Windows. Bigger userbase would help Linux's development process, and would incline developers to code natively for Linux.

Everybody uses Windows because it was the only affordable business system when it was started in the 80s. Unix cost a shit ton of money and was only built for mainframes, and there weren't any other viable alternatives. They kept control of the market by somehow convincing companies that Windows was better because it cost more money. I've been using computers since before my hands were large enough to touch type on a keyboard, and I've used just about every operating system in existence (at least since, say, 1975). I've also worked professionally as a programmer.

Windows architecture has been flawed from the start, and even those inculcated with it complain about it all the time. The APIs are a nightmare, and the languages themselves are poorly designed. The systems architecture is even more of a nightmare, see the inevitable 'restart the machine to fix X' solution used by every Windows IT department in the world.

In terms of backwards compatibility, things written for Linux from 1995 would most likely work perfectly with a modern machine. Granted, there have been some user facing changes to architecture in the past 20 years, but even those changes are well documented and would make porting most software (esp. business software) trivial. Yes, the internal OS API changes fairly often, but that hasn't dissuaded almost every OEM from hiring linux kernel devs to keep their linux drivers up to date and working.

In addition to this, most serious companies already use linux internally in all of their products, if not in their business operations. Everything from power plants to boats to cable set top boxes run linux underneath whatever proprietary user interface they develop internally.

Gaming is about the only thing linux doesn't do incredibly well right now, and that is mostly because of industry reluctance to retrain their programmers on OpenGL rather than DirectX, and the graphics card OEMs being the last electronics manufacturers who almost outright refuse to work with kernel devs to build drivers that can use the full capacity of their high end graphics cards. Despite this the kernel dev community is making progress reverse engineering the drivers for these advanced graphics cards.

As for Linux not having a Windows compatibility layer, here you may not have the requisite knowledge to understand the problem. There are several ways in which Linux makes completely different design decisions than Windows. To support Windows executables natively would basically require a virtual machine running a Windows box (an option a good number of people utilize) in order to simulate the differences (in most cases bad or insecure differences). The reason why this isn't done by the kernel dev team? They're interested in operating systems, not holding the hand of every user that wants to be able to run Internet Explorer natively on Linux. There are groups of people who work on these things, with great success, but to ask the Linux kernel team to support native Windows emulation is like asking Ferrari to build a subcompact because that's what you like.
